title: Principles of Epidemiology
description: Measures of disease frequency and association, surveillance, outbreak investigation, screening test evaluation and causation.

topics.title: Measures of Disease Frequency
topics.summary: Rates, ratios and proportions; incidence and prevalence; mortality and morbidity indicators.

notes.b: Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations, and the application of this study to control health problems. Incidence measures new cases: cumulative incidence (risk) = new cases during a period ÷ population at risk at the start; incidence rate (density) = new cases ÷ person-time at risk. Prevalence measures existing cases: point prevalence = all cases at a point in time ÷ total population. Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration of disease — so a treatment that prolongs survival without cure increases prevalence. Attack rate is the cumulative incidence during an outbreak.
k: Incidence: new cases; prevalence: existing cases
Attack rate: incidence during an outbreak

notes.b: Crude death rate = deaths per 1,000 population per year. Case fatality rate = deaths from a disease ÷ cases of that disease (× 100%) — a measure of severity (e.g. Lassa fever CFR in Nigeria is often around 15–20% among confirmed cases). Infant mortality rate = infant deaths (< 1 year) per 1,000 live births; neonatal mortality rate (< 28 days) per 1,000 live births; under-five mortality rate per 1,000 live births; maternal mortality ratio per 100,000 live births. Age standardisation (direct or indirect) allows fair comparison between populations with different age structures; the standardised mortality ratio (SMR) = observed ÷ expected deaths.

topics.title: Measures of Association and Impact
topics.summary: Relative risk, odds ratio, attributable risk, population attributable fraction and number needed to treat.

notes.b: Relative risk (RR) = incidence in exposed ÷ incidence in unexposed (from cohort studies and trials): RR = 1 no association; > 1 increased risk; < 1 protective. The odds ratio (OR) = (a × d) ÷ (b × c) from a 2×2 table; it is used in case–control studies and approximates the RR when the disease is rare. Confidence intervals that include 1 indicate no statistically significant association. Hazard ratios come from survival analysis.

Attributable risk (risk difference) = incidence in exposed − incidence in unexposed; it indicates the excess risk due to exposure. Attributable risk percent = AR ÷ incidence in exposed × 100. Population attributable risk (fraction) estimates the proportion of disease in the whole population due to the exposure — useful for public health planning. In trials: absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate − experimental event rate; number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ ARR; relative risk reduction = ARR ÷ control event rate.

topics.title: Surveillance and Outbreak Investigation
topics.summary: Types of surveillance, IDSR in Nigeria, notifiable diseases and steps in outbreak investigation.

notes.b: Public health surveillance is the ongoing systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for action. Types: passive (routine reports from health facilities — cheap but incomplete), active (health workers seek cases — e.g. polio acute flaccid paralysis surveillance), sentinel (selected sites), syndromic and event-based surveillance. Nigeria uses the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) strategy coordinated by the NCDC, with immediately notifiable diseases (e.g. cholera, Lassa fever, measles, meningitis, yellow fever, acute flaccid paralysis, avian influenza, Ebola, COVID-19, anthrax, mpox) and weekly/monthly reporting through SORMAS and DHIS2. Epidemic thresholds (alert and action) trigger responses.
k: Immediately notifiable: cholera, Lassa, measles, CSM, AFP

notes.b: An outbreak (epidemic) is the occurrence of cases clearly in excess of normal expectancy. Steps: prepare for fieldwork; confirm the existence of an outbreak; verify the diagnosis (clinical and laboratory); establish a case definition (suspected, probable, confirmed — by person, place and time) and find cases (line list); describe the outbreak (epidemic curve by time, spot map by place, characteristics of persons); develop hypotheses; test hypotheses (analytical studies — cohort or case–control); implement control and prevention measures (which should start early, not wait for the end); communicate findings; and maintain surveillance. A point-source epidemic curve shows a sharp rise and fall within one incubation period; a propagated (person-to-person) curve shows successive peaks.

topics.title: Screening and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
topics.summary: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios and screening biases.

notes.b: From a 2×2 table comparing a test with a gold standard: sensitivity = true positives ÷ all with disease (TP/(TP+FN)) — the ability to detect disease; specificity = true negatives ÷ all without disease (TN/(TN+FP)). A highly sensitive test, when negative, rules OUT disease (SnNout); a highly specific test, when positive, rules IN disease (SpPin). Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP/(TP+FP); negative predictive value (NPV) = TN/(TN+FN). Predictive values depend on prevalence: as prevalence falls, PPV falls and NPV rises. Likelihood ratios (LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity)) do not depend on prevalence.

Screening detects disease early in apparently healthy people; positive screening tests are followed by diagnostic tests. Serial testing (both tests must be positive) increases specificity; parallel testing (either test positive) increases sensitivity — e.g. HIV testing algorithms use serial testing with confirmatory assays. Biases in evaluating screening: lead-time bias (earlier diagnosis appears to lengthen survival without changing time of death), length-time bias (screening preferentially detects slow-growing disease) and overdiagnosis (detecting disease that would never cause harm). Screening programmes should meet the Wilson–Jungner criteria.

topics.title: Causation and Disease Transmission
topics.summary: Bradford Hill criteria, chain of transmission, herd immunity and R0.

notes.b: Association does not prove causation. The Bradford Hill criteria help judge whether an association is causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality (the cause must precede the effect — the only essential criterion), biological gradient (dose–response), plausibility, coherence, experiment (reversibility) and analogy. Alternative explanations for an association are chance, bias and confounding. Causes may be necessary (must be present — e.g. Mycobacterium tuberculosis for TB) and/or sufficient.

Infectious disease terms: reservoir (where the agent normally lives — humans, animals such as Mastomys rats for Lassa, environment), carrier (infected without symptoms but infectious, e.g. typhoid carriers), incubation period, period of communicability, and modes of transmission (direct contact, droplet, airborne, vehicle-borne such as water and food, vector-borne, vertical). The basic reproduction number R0 is the average number of secondary cases produced by one case in a fully susceptible population (measles ≈ 12–18); an epidemic grows when the effective reproduction number R > 1. Herd immunity threshold ≈ 1 − 1/R0 (about 92–95% for measles), achieved mainly through vaccination. Zoonoses are diseases transmitted from animals (Lassa fever, rabies, anthrax, mpox); One Health links human, animal and environmental health.
